title: Your phone’s GPS only works because it corrects for relativity
body: GPS finds your position by timing signals from satellites, so their atomic clocks must agree with clocks on the ground to within billionths of a second. Einstein’s relativity spoils that: combined, its effects make the satellite clocks run fast by about 38 microseconds a day. That sounds tiny, but light travels more than 11 km in that time, so without a correction your position would be off by kilometres within a single day.

slides.question: How high above Earth do GPS satellites orbit?
slides.explanation: About 20,200 km up, in medium Earth orbit: 50 times higher than the ISS, yet well below geostationary satellites. Up there gravity is weaker, so the satellite clocks tick faster.

slides.question: Overall, by how many microseconds a day do GPS satellite clocks run fast?
slides.explanation: About 38 microseconds a day: their speed slows them by about 7, but weaker gravity 20,000 km up speeds them by about 45. Light covers more than 11 km in 38 microseconds.

slides.heading: What relativity does to a GPS clock, per day
slides.note: Microseconds gained each day: speed costs 7, weaker gravity adds 45, net 38 fast

slides.heading: Speed slows the clock
slides.text: Orbiting at nearly 4 km/s, each satellite clock runs slow by about 7 microseconds a day, as special relativity predicts for moving clocks.

slides.heading: Weak gravity speeds it up
slides.text: About 20,000 km up, gravity is weaker, and general relativity says clocks there tick faster: about 45 microseconds a day gained. Net result: +38.

slides.heading: The fix is built in
slides.text: Before launch, the satellite clocks are tuned to tick at 10.22999999543 MHz instead of 10.23 MHz, so once in orbit they match clocks on Earth.

source.label: Wikipedia: Error analysis for the Global Positioning System
